title: Drinking Coffee, Mate, and Very Hot Beverages
authors: IARC Working Group on the Evaluation of Carcinogenic Risks to Humans
journal: IARC Monographs on the Evaluation of Carcinogenic Risks to Humans, volume 116
population: Working Group of 23 members from ten countries, one unable to attend, Lyon, 24 to 31 May 2016; more than 1000 studies of drinking coffee, mate and very hot beverages and cancer at more than 20 sites
funder: This programme has been supported since 1982 by Cooperative Agreement U01 CA33193 with the United States National Cancer Institute, Department of Health and Human Services. Additional support has been provided since 1986 by the European Commission Directorate-General for Employment, Social Affairs, and Inclusion, and since 1992 by the United States National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences. The contents of this volume are solely the responsibility of the Working Group.
authorConflicts: No pertinent interests are listed for Working Group members. Observers, who did not draft text or take part in the evaluations, included Thomas Hatzold for the Institute for Scientific Information on Coffee, an organisation whose members include six of the major European coffee companies (employed by Mondelez International until 2015 and holding its stock options), and Alan Leviton for the National Coffee Association, a US trade association for which he has provided consulting services.
result: There is inadequate evidence in humans and in experimental animals for the carcinogenicity of drinking coffee. There is evidence suggesting lack of carcinogenicity of drinking coffee in humans for cancers of the pancreas, liver, female breast, uterine endometrium and prostate; inverse associations were observed with cancers of the liver and uterine endometrium. Drinking coffee is not classifiable as to its carcinogenicity to humans (Group 3).
